(Image: Wikipedia) The Odyssey is one of the oldest and most lasting works in Western literature, so it’s no surprise that Christopher Nolan is the latest in a long line of people–authors, artists, and filmmakers–who seek to “adapt” it. Whether Nolan’s work is, indeed, a good adaptation of the original is both a separate question and one open to debate. Polish author Roman Brandstaetter (1906-87) (Image: Wikipedia) Let me, instead, focus on another adaptation. Polish author and dramatist Roman Brandstaetter (1906-1987) grew up in a solidly Jewish home, his grandfather a distinguished rabbi. Thoroughly immersed in Judaism, he quickly made a mark for himself in the 1930s as a Polish and Jewish thinker and writer. A process began during World War II in Jerusalem that resulted in Brandstaetter’s postwar baptism. He refused to call it a “conversion” because he insisted that his entry into Catholicism was not a turning from his Jewish roots but their fulfillment. His most notable work is a four-volume work, Jezus z Nazaretu [Jesus of Nazareth], whose life he retells in Christian terms but also wholly grounded in the thought, mentality, and culture of a first-century Jew. Brandstaetter would be included among the major writers of the 20th-century Polish literary canon. But that does not mean he was readily accepted nor had an easy time of things. Any author in post-World War II Poland would have to contend with the dictates of socialist thinking: an observant Catholic was already suspect. A Jew might also rub various people the wrong way: Catholics who doubted the authenticity of his faith; Communists who played the antisemitism card; Jews who thought Brandstaetter’s Christianity was a betrayal. And still he persisted … and succeeded. His literary corpus includes 20 plays, including several adaptations of classical Greek stories: Antigone, Medea, Iphigenia, and, of course, Odysseus. “Odys płaczący” [Odysseus Weeping] is one of his shorter plays, one that reconsiders the whole Odysseus legend, especially the legend of the hero, the patience of his wife, Penelope, and the fate of their son, Telemachus. In the Homeric tradition, Odysseus is King of Ithaca, who goes to Troy to fight in the famous Trojan War. Despite a decade-long siege, Troy remained impregnable. In response, Odysseus devised the scheme of building a giant wooden horse to leave behind as a “gift.” The Trojans would bring into their city, allowing the Greeks hiding inside it to emerge and sack the place. Odysseus and his men plunder the city, intending to return to Greece with their booty. Boastfully planning to return home, his return is impeded by the gods who punish his hubris, his men who make bad decisions, and his own tarrying. By the time he returns to Ithaca, he has been gone twenty years, his wife and home beset by suitors convinced he is dead who want to marry his wife and divide his wealth. In Homer’s version, Odysseus, together with his son, Telemachus, slays the suitors, and the home is happy ever after. Brandstaetter presents a somewhat different reality in a four-character play: Odysseus, Penelope, Telemachus, and a Greek chorus. For most of the play, Odysseus is presented as a “drifter,” a man unrecognized by his wife, who is busy spinning. (In Homer’s original, Penelope weaves a shroud. She puts off her suitors by saying she would marry once she finishes it–only to unweave it at night.) The Drifter is impressed by what he has observed of Penelope and Telemachus and relays news about Odysseus in the third person, including assuring Penelope that Odysseus loves her. She wants to believe him, but she also doubts whether he is just another enterprising soul with a story who hopes somehow to profit by it. The course of the discussion, however, turns on a deeper question. Thomas Wolfe broached it in his great 1940 novel, You Can’t Go Home Again , when he answered negatively whether one can ever really go home again. Penelope awaits a man who left twenty years ago. Her memory and vision of that man are, in a sense, frozen in time. A warrior king sallied forth from Ithaca to do epic battle, gain great loot, and return with riches and honor. Would one imagine this drifter—whose “feet and clothing are covered in dust”—was that man? Even before revealing himself, the Drifter asks Penelope, “Of which Odysseus do you speak?” Yes, he remembers the brave and handsome Odysseus who went off to Troy, spilling blood as liberally as wine. But does she want to know “how the Odysseus who wanders the world looks? … He is old and grey. The sunset is in his gaze. He is as tired as a shadow.” He tells her bluntly that “a man living beyond the reach of our sight and our touch is but a cruel illusion,” the fossil of our memories but not necessarily the living human being. Like a pond in the palace of Ithaca that used to be surrounded by now desiccated cypresses, “they died because their souls were their own reflections in water that is not there today.” As their conversation progresses, Penelope seems unshakably attached to the past. It moves beyond Odysseus and Penelope to their child and Penelope’s concerns that, unlike his father (or at least her memory of him), Telemachus is perhaps too sensitive to be a king. When the Drifter presses to speak to the boy and tell him about his encounters with his father, Penelope refuses … and the Drifter reveals who he is. “I am Odysseus! I am Odysseus!” He confesses he has been “born twice.” The first time was in Ithaca, the boy who grew up to be the hero that lay siege to Troy. The second was born the day “when I came to know the world’s hells. I experienced suffering and saw suffering so great that even the wisest among us could not … understand its magnitude.” He disavows the man who “murdered people for three days and three nights without interruption … [who] killed girls who were like young olive trees, [who] smashed the heads of infants on marble steps and killed the incapacitated elderly with a sword thrust in the back.” “Born twice” alludes to the Christian mystery of being “born again”—something not possible by human agency but divine grace. Penelope dismisses that man: “Leave! You are lying, drifter!” And that Drifter withdraws with but two words: “Farewell, Penelope!” The play concludes with the Chorus asking Penelope, “Are the ladies to sit down at the looms and weave a linen wedding dress?” She answers no. “What do you intend to do?” the Chorus asks. “Wait for Odysseus!” “But that was Odyseeus, after all, Penelope.” The curtain drops as “Penelope sits down motionlessly, like a stone, full of the weight of choked back weeping.” Brandstaetter’s adaptation perhaps reflects aspects of his own life. The author who made a name for himself as a distinguished Jewish writer in Hebrew in interwar Poland never went back to those days or those writings. That chapter of his life was like a closed book. But the play is not primarily an autobiography. Odysseus the Returnee, the Drifter, is in some sense … Everyman. Everyman for whom life continues, even when those who have surrounded or known or think they have known him discover that the person they think they knew is gone. How do we treat a person whose life has been changed by the passage of time? Do we accept what they have become? Or do we insist on forcing them into the Procrustean bed of our own preconceptions, as if time froze when they stepped out of our daily lives? How often do we overlay our expectations on another, and then reject the other because they continued to live? How often are marriages and families burdened by the weight of past expectations, of ideas and persons which time has passed by? And, instead of receiving the moment as it is, how often do we try to yoke what is to expectations of what has been? And how often do those expectations accompany a refusal to forgive and forget the past to live in the present, the now? Conversion itself also involves putting on a new man, a new man who may not meet the expectations of others accustomed to the old man. The lessons of Odysseus remain vital some 2,700 years after the Odyssey may have been written. They remain vital because they illumine constant challenges of human life, not because they might be just fodder for action heroes. In that task, Brandstaetter’s “Odysseus Weeping” gives us grist for Christian reflection on a great, if flawed, pagan hero. (Note: Brandstaetter’s “Odysseus Weeping” is untranslated from Polish; translations here are by the author, all rights reserved.) And to the most recent clown using the title of one of his great works for a ridiculous film. Read Homer. Reply Yes, reading books offer greater depth and nuance than watching films. This film title–Odysseus–is not the same as the book–The Odyssey. In the US, the book is in the public domain, so there is no copyright restriction on using the name or the title. Dp you really think Nolan is a clown? Why? I presume you’ve seen the film so that you can qualify it as ridiculous? What about it led you to conclude so? Reply Error in above. The book title is the same as the film title. Reply Thank you, Professor, for this write-up, most specially the play and its author. I was wondering how Nolan would approach the epic. Nolan is one of those rare directors who sees deeply and depicts his insights well. He was baptized Catholic but reportedly does not now practice. His films (Dunkirk, Interstellar, Dark Knight) are worthy although Dark Knight is a bit too dark. I’m thankful that his movies typically differ from the junk Hollywood serves as ‘art’ or ‘entertainment.’ The last film I saw was probably Dunkirk, so I’m looking forward to Odysseus. No. We cannot go home again. Didn’t the epic’s happy ending seem somewhat unbelievable? Perhaps I should re-read it. The warrior Odysseus, returning home after so many unbelievably precipitous calamities, as the cause of his delay. All along, the inkling that he couldn’t easily return home after the war that he’d seen kept nudging me. Fought because of an unfaithful woman,—why would Odysseus have any reason to think Penelope would be any different? I’m happy, looking forward to what I hope will be a thoughtful, wholesome, realistic story well done, in an air-conditioned theatre since Seattle is forecast to have 85 degree days most days next week. Thanks again. Reply Excellent piece & reflection Dr. G. Reply And, instead of receiving the moment as it is, how often do we try to yoke what is to expectations of what has been? And how often do those expectations accompany a refusal to forgive and forget the past to live in the present, the now? (Grondelski). A dynamic many of us suffer. Seeking to relive the past rather than the realization, We cannot alter history. The Apostle Paul made the point that he left the past behind and looked toward what’s ahead. Reply What Francis of Paola had to say in A.D. 1486 about the past is that resentful memories of evil, at least, are unnecessary baggage: “Memory of an injury is itself wrong. It adds to our anger, nurtures our sin and hates what is good. It is a rusty arrow and poison for the soul. It puts all virtue to flight. It is like a worm in the mind: it confuses our speech and tears to shreds our petitions to God. It is foreign to charity: it remains planted in the soul like a nail. It is indeed a daily death” (Letter by Saint Francis of Paolo, in “Liturgy of the Hours,” for April 2 in Vol. II). Reply Thank you for the reference. I will use it. Reply Far be it for me to disagree with a saint, but it’s not always that simple. A grave injustice should never be forgotten. Opportunity to redress a past evil may present in the future where a resolution is an ultimate good for all souls involved. Reply Yes, there are occasions when remembrance of a persecution, injury inflicted upon us can be spiritually utilized in imitation of Christ by offering ourselves as an oblation for their conversion and salvation. As such we contribute to the sufferings lacking by Christ for the Mystical Body (Col. 1:24). By our willingness to offer our sufferings for sinners, in specific those who have harmed us, we carry on the work of Christ in the world. Reply I don’t think St. John of the Cross would disagree when memories cause us to do good. I think those type of memories is what you are addressing…memories where you have caused an injustice? Memories carrying negative loads because of others’ injustices toward us are problematic. If painful, injurious memories arouse wrath, thought of revenge, or other evils because of injustices we’ve suffered, we do well to allow their ‘purification’ so we may grow in union with Christ. If we have been the cause of injustice toward others, yes, our resolve and remembrance may help redress and atone. In both cases, St. John points to HOPE for the present and for the future which basically grants to God our efforts to heal. Some of his movies have been disappointing. “IntersteLLar,” for example, began promisingly only to become increasingly ridulous to the point that I thought my eyes were going to roll right out of my head. So I approached “The Odyssey” with a bit of trepidation. But I have to say, Nolan really knocked this one out of the park, and I’m not going to fault him for taking a three year hiatus from filmmaking, as he says he plans to do. Sure, he could have stuck very strictly to the source material, including a lot more gore not to mention Odysseus’ year-long sexual romp with Circe. But that would have made for a MUCH longer and unmarketable film. Like Peter Jackson and his “Lord of the Rings” movies, Nolan made some hard choices in order to craft a convincing epic tale. It’s already outgrossed “Disclosure Day.” Again, this is an R-rated movie based on a Greek epic and it’s close to three hours long. Only Nolan could have made this into a box office guarantee. I thought it was absolutely magnificent. Share this article paywall-free Email Copy Link Is the rush to the Arctic Circle really the smartest way to beat the summer heat, or is it just the fastest way to burn through your savings? The travel industry is obsessed with “coolcations” — flocking to Scandinavia, Alaska and Iceland as global temperatures rise. But many of the cool destinations have become overcrowded tourist traps. Maybe the smart move this summer is a “hotcation”: Head straight for the heat, where luxury is cheap and the air conditioning is cold. The cold hard truth about coolcations The marketing pitch for a coolcation is simple: Escape the sweltering summer by heading north. But the reality can be a sweaty, expensive mess. Terence Leung, a marketing manager from Calgary, followed the herd to Scandinavia last July. He expected a quiet getaway, but found rooms had doubled in price and ferry routes were booked. Worse, he ran into a heat wave in Oslo. “I was in hotels without air conditioning,” he recalls. “People started pacing the hallways at midnight, unable to sleep.” Adam Tank, a tech executive from Kansas City, Mo., had an even worse experience in Iceland. Trying to beat the late summer heat, he rented a car to drive the island’s famous ring road. After a mudslide delayed his arrival in a northern village, he got lost and asked a police officer for directions. “They said yes to my request and asked me to follow them,” says Tank. But instead of leading him to his vacation rental, the police drove him 30 minutes out of town into the middle of nowhere. “The cops clearly weren’t thrilled with the amount of tourism and didn’t want us in their town,” he says. Is the coolcation just a marketing gimmick? According to industry insiders, the coolcation trend isn’t an organic response to climate change, but a calculated move to sell inventory. “It is a classic inventory problem solved with premium branding,” says Delbert Lee, a former vice president of sales for a tour company. He explains that companies identified destinations with low summer demand and repackaged them as exclusive escapes, charging 30% to 40% more for infrastructure that was never built to handle peak crowds during the summer. Samuel Huang, CEO of an ad agency in Singapore, agrees. His firm has been tracking worldwide advertising content for years, and it’s seen a 30% to 40% increase in ad spend targeting warmer regions with arctic imagery. “This marketing push creates an artificial scarcity that inflates prices for subpar infrastructure,” Huang says. He notes that negative online reviews for these destinations are climbing by 30% quarter-over-quarter. Lorena Basualdo, a luxury travel adviser who specializes in Italian vacations, points out that northern gateways have brief summers and limited transport slots. “You’ll still find limited AC, small elevators, scarce shade structures, undersized water stations and transit timetables that can’t stretch during surges,” she warns. The case for the ‘hotcation’ While everyone else is fighting for a view of a glacier, the “hotcation” — embracing the heat in places like Phoenix, Dubai or Madrid — is emerging as a value play. “A luxury hotel in Dubai or Phoenix operates at a loss during its summer offseason,” explains Lee. He says these properties offer 50% to 70% discounts not as a special deal, but as a baseline necessity. Amanda Persi, CEO of The Getaway Co., agrees that hot destinations can offer better value, but warns that travelers must be honest with themselves about the heat. “Sightseeing all day in the sun isn’t always realistic,” Persi says. She notes that if you treat the trip less like a checklist and more like a lifestyle — slowing down and resting by the pool during the day — the experience can be magical. Leung, who felt burned by his Scandinavian adventure, eventually tried this approach. “During peak heat, Phoenix and Madrid were empty and cheap,” he says. The resorts had shaded areas, ice-cold air and open pools. “Heat can be managed,” he adds. “Scarcity and crowds can’t.” I’ve spent a few summers in hot-weather destinations like Phoenix and the Florida Keys, and I’m with Leung on this one. The tourists leave, and the rates drop faster than the temperature in your air-conditioned hotel room. But is it a fair comparison? Of course, not everyone agrees that swapping a glacier for a desert pool is a valid comparison. Jared Sternberg, founder of Gondwana Ecotours, argues that comparing Alaska to Phoenix is meaningless. “One is about immersion in wild landscapes, long daylight, wildlife and remoteness; the other is about urban comfort,” Sternberg says. Experts also defend the high prices of remote destinations. Sternberg notes that Alaska faces significantly higher infrastructure costs and shorter operating seasons. Andrew Harrison, a travel advisor with OvationNetwork, points out that the high price tags in Scandinavia reflect the reality of the local economy. “Scandinavia has the highest fuel and labor costs in the world, and the prices for the trip reflect that,” Harrison says. Travelers are voting with their wallets Despite the warnings, it looks like travelers are trending toward hotcation this summer. Lauren McCormick, a spokeswoman for the travel insurance company Squaremouth, says interest in hot-weather destinations for this summer has outpaced demand for cool-weather getaways. Squaremouth’s data shows interest in Costa Rica has jumped nearly 41% and Italy is up 24%, while searches for Norway have dropped by nearly 18%. Still, she warns that a hotcation comes with risks. “Hot destinations, especially during summer months, bring added health and safety considerations, such as heat-related illnesses,” she says. McCormick recommends either travel insurance or medical insurance with at least $50,000 in medical coverage and $100,000 for medical evacuation. How to travel smarter this summer If you want to avoid the coolcation trap but aren’t ready to bake in the desert, there are middle-ground solutions. Wait for the shoulder. Mitch Krayton, a Denver travel agent, warns against the Arctic or Alaska in high summer. “Go in the shoulder season or offseason to avoid the crowds and get the best rates,” he says. For Alaska, that means September and October. Look for alternative cool spots. Sam Bruce, co-founder of Much Better Adventures, suggests looking at cooler places outside the obvious circuit, like Estonia, where you can enjoy milder summers without the overcrowding. Check the AC. Don’t assume a hotel is equipped for a heat wave. Basualdo says you must ensure your room has an air conditioner. “Filter out the ones that don’t,” she says. So this summer, you might not want to hang out with the cool kids heading north with the herd. They’re putting a strain on the infrastructure, and ironically, they may suffer through a heat wave without air conditioning. Ultimately, the hottest summer destination might literally be the hottest summer destination. Christopher Elliott is an author, consumer advocate and journalist. Contact him at chris@elliott.org . Beállítom Donald Trump amerikai elnök hétfőn arról posztolt, hogy az ukrajnai háború súlyosan érintette az orosz energiaszektort, valamint sürgette a konfliktus lezárását. „Oroszország sajnálatos módon elvesztette az irányítást a dízelolaj-ipara felett az Ukrajnával vívott háború miatt. Számos dízelfinomítójukat felrobbantották, és ezek, legalábbis átmenetileg, működésképtelenekké váltak” – írta Trump hétfői Truth Social-bejegyzésében . Az amerikai elnök szerint véget kell vetni ennek a „nevetséges és soha véget nem érő” ukrajnai háborúnak. „Az egész világ szenved, miközben havonta 25 ezer ember, többségük katona, hal meg” – tette hozzá. Trump azután posztolt, hogy Ukrajna az oroszországi választások harmadik napján több száz drónnal nagyszabású támadást indított Moszkva és környéke ellen. Az akcióban legalább három ember meghalt, és megrongálódott az a finomító , amelyet Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök Oroszország egyik „legfontosabb olajipari létesítményének” nevezett. Az ukrán elnök Trump posztjára reagálva azt írta X-en , hogy országa kész leállítani az Oroszország elleni támadásokat, ha a Kreml is megteszi ugyanezt. „Ukrajna energetikai szektorának, kritikus infrastruktúrájának és élelmiszer-exportjának meg kell szűnnie orosz célpontnak lenni, és ez részünkről megfelelő deeszkalációs lépésekhez fog vezetni. Lehetségesek a megoldások” – közölte Zelenszkij. Szerinte a tárgyalások folytatódnak, és az asztalon vannak olyan elképzelések, amelyek közelebb hozhatják a békét, kezdve az erőteljes deeszkalációs lépésekkel. Zelenszkij vasárnap telefonon beszélt Trumppal, és egy magas rangú ukrán tisztviselő a Financial Timesnak azt mondta, hogy a dízel is szóba került. A két vezető várhatóan kedden találkozik az ENSZ Közgyűlése magas szintű hetének keretében. Szergej Lavrov orosz külügyminiszter pedig Washingtonban lesz a héten, és vélhetően találkozik amerikai kollégájával, Marco Rubioval. A Guardian szerint Trump arra fogja sürgetni Zelenszkijt, hogy állapodjanak meg az energetikai célpontok elleni támadások beszüntetéséről. Az amerikai elnök azért akarja erre rábeszélni az ukrán vezetőt, mert a világ dízelárai megugrottak az iráni és az ukrajnai háború miatt. Az Egyesült Államokban hétfőn rekordot döntött a dízel átlagára: egy gallon 6,5 dollár volt, szemben az egy évvel korábbi 3,19 dollárral. Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty Images View image in fullscreen FBI agents visited Matthew Unglesbee’s home and discovered another empty envelope addressed to a Congress member’s Washington DC office, officials say. Photograph: Finn Gomez/Getty Images US crime Illinois man arrested after allegedly sending suspicious powder to Congress members using his return address Matthew Unglesbee admitted to sending the letters to four unidentified politicians, officials say Richard Luscombe Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.55 EDT Last modified on Tue 27 Oct 2026 09.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Illinois man accused of sending letters containing suspicious white powder to four members of Congress has been arrested after he allegedly wrote his own name and return address on the envelopes, according to authorities. Matthew Unglesbee, 36, of Quincy, remained in the custody of US marshals on Tuesday on federal charges of perpetrating a hoax and sending threatening communications through the mail. In an eight-page criminal complaint unsealed on Monday, Charis Hobbs – a taskforce agent with the FBI’s Springfield office – said Unglesbee admitted during an interview on Sunday that he sent the letters to the four unidentified politicians. Unglesbee told the agent that the substance he placed inside the envelopes was salt – because it “kind of looks like” anthrax, the complaint said. Preliminary testing did not reveal the presence of any biological or chemical toxin. “Each letter contained a white granular substance and a handwritten letter which read ‘ha ha’,” the court filing said. A letter to an unnamed US senator also contained granules and read “Hah enjoy the gift”. On each of the four white, letter-sized envelopes, the agent said, Unglesbee wrote his name and home address in Quincy. None of the staffers who handled the letters at any of the four Congress members’ offices in northern Illinois opened the envelopes, the complaint said. The offices had alerted each other to look out for mailings with Unglesbee’s name on them. FBI personnel “trained in handling weapons of mass destruction, and threats of biochemical toxins” were sent to three of the politicians’ offices on Wednesday after staff called authorities, and hazardous materials (hazmat) response teams attended two of them. Having retrieved the communications with Unglesbee’s address on them, FBI agents visited his home, where they discovered another envelope – empty and addressed, but not sent, to one of the same Congress member’s Washington DC office. The suspect told investigators that he mailed four letters “after hearing someone in a restaurant mention the news story of other letters being sent”, the filing said. Earlier in October, the FBI and US Postal Inspection Service said they were investigating multiple reports of suspicious letters sent to state officials and election offices across the country. Unglesbee denied participating in the other suspicious mailings. But he allegedly told investigators that he anticipated the Congress members would “take it serious” because the powder he sent could be perceived to be anthrax, which he said he knew was dangerous and would cause hazmat teams to have to respond. “Unglesbee claimed he was joking but recognized the recipients would not know he was joking and could perceive it as a threat,” the complaint said. In a justice department press release on Monday announcing Unglesbee’s arrest, Ryan Presley, special agent in charge of the FBI’s Springfield field office, said authorities were focused on “keeping our public institutions safe from intimidation”. He said: “Mailing unknown substances to congressional offices creates fear and disrupts the public institutions vital to our democracy. We, along with our partners, will remain vigilant in identifying and holding accountable those whose actions threaten to intimidate public officials or disrupt our democratic systems.” Unglesbee was tentatively scheduled to appear for a detention hearing on Wednesday afternoon in federal court in Springfield.
